title: "The No-U-Turn Sampler"

The [HMC page](hamiltonian-monte-carlo.qmd#leapfrog-integration) required us to
choose two numbers: a step size $\epsilon$ and a number of leapfrog steps $L$.
Their product controls the approximate length of the trajectory. A short
trajectory leaves us close to the starting point and brings back the
random-walk problem. A very long trajectory may pass through useful new
regions, turn around, and travel back toward its starting point while spending
additional computation.

The step size can be learned during warmup by comparing numerical energy error
with a target acceptance rate. The appropriate number of steps is harder to
fix because one trajectory may need to travel farther than another. The
[**No-U-Turn Sampler (NUTS)**](https://bruno.nicenboim.me/bayescogsci/ch-introstan.html)
lets each trajectory grow until its motion begins to reverse. Hoffman and
Gelman ([2014](https://jmlr.org/papers/v15/hoffman14a.html)) introduced the
original algorithm; Stan uses a multinomial variant described in its
[reference manual](https://mc-stan.org/docs/reference-manual/mcmc.html).

The name describes the stopping intuition, but the actual algorithm must do
more than look at the last two points. It grows a balanced tree of trajectory
states in forward and backward directions, checks completed subtrees for
turning, excludes numerically invalid states, and selects one eligible state
for the next Markov-chain iteration. We will build up those pieces from a
one-dimensional path before inspecting the amount of trajectory work in the
passage-level fit.

## Growing and stopping a trajectory

Begin in one dimension at $q=0$ with positive momentum. The trajectory might
visit $q=1$, then $q=2$, then $q=2.4$. If its momentum later becomes negative,
the trajectory is moving back toward the span it already covered. Continuing
far enough could return it near $q=0$. NUTS is designed to stop before that
return erases the benefit of the outward movement.

For a multidimensional path, “moving back” cannot be read from one coordinate.
We instead compare the displacement between the two endpoints with the
momentum at each endpoint. The dot product is positive when the momentum has a
component pointing along the endpoint displacement and negative when it has a
component pointing back across that span. The [dot-product discussion](../random-variables-and-distributions/variance-and-covariance.qmd#vectors-matrices-and-covariance)
explains why the sign measures directional alignment.

NUTS extends an HMC path forward or backward and organizes candidate states in a balanced binary tree. Increasing tree depth by one doubles the intended path length, though a turning condition or divergence may stop it early. The tree constructs one transition; its internal states are not additional posterior draws.

Let $q^-$ and $q^+$ be the trajectory endpoints and define

$$
\Delta q=q^+-q^-.
$$

An endpoint turning check examines

$$
\Delta q^\mathsf TM^{-1}\rho^-
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
\Delta q^\mathsf TM^{-1}\rho^+.
$$

When one becomes negative, momentum at that endpoint points back across the
path. The factor $M^{-1}$ converts momentum to velocity using the
[mass-matrix relationship](mass-matrix-geometry.qmd#general-kinetic-energy),
so the check is carried out in the adapted geometry rather than in arbitrary
raw coordinate scales. Stan also checks completed subtrees. It selects one
eligible state with weights related to $\exp\{-H(q,\rho)\}$, rather than
automatically taking the final endpoint.

A one-dimensional schematic makes the doubling rule concrete:

| tree depth | intended leapfrog states | question before further growth |
|---:|---:|---|
| 0 | 1 | Is this state eligible? | <!-- dqr-allow: algorithm-setting -->
| 1 | 2 | Do the endpoint momenta still point along the span? | <!-- dqr-allow: algorithm-setting -->
| 2 | 4 | Has either completed subtree turned? | <!-- dqr-allow: algorithm-setting -->
| 3 | 8 | Would another doubling reverse direction or encounter an energy failure? | <!-- dqr-allow: algorithm-setting -->

Suppose $q^-<q^+$. If the right-end momentum becomes negative, then $(q^+-q^-)M^{-1}\rho^+<0$: the path at the right endpoint is moving back toward the left. Internal tree states helped construct this one transition; counting them all as posterior draws would overweight a single trajectory. Stan's multinomial selection instead chooses one eligible state using energy-related weights.

## Passage-level Student-t model tree lengths

We now examine four chains for the 55-passage Student-$t$ model. Each chain
used 750 warmup iterations followed by 1,000 retained iterations, with
`adapt_delta = 0.90` and `max_treedepth = 10`. The tree depths tell us how much
leapfrog work each retained transition required while targeting the posterior
defined on the [Stan page](stan.qmd#the-complete-program).

```{r}
#| label: load-provo-nuts-diagnostics
library(ggplot2)
library(posterior)

provo <- read.csv("data/provo/passage-summaries.csv", stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
y <- provo$noun_minus_verb_log_ffd
cache <- readRDS(
  "data/provo/provo-stan-draw-cache.rds"
)
diagnostics <- as.data.frame(as_draws_df(cache$production_diagnostics))

nuts_summary <- do.call(rbind, lapply(
  split(diagnostics, diagnostics$.chain),
  function(chain_data) data.frame(
    chain = chain_data$.chain[1],
    draws = nrow(chain_data),
    median_tree_depth = median(chain_data$treedepth__),
    maximum_tree_depth = max(chain_data$treedepth__),
    median_leapfrog_steps = median(chain_data$n_leapfrog__),
    maximum_leapfrog_steps = max(chain_data$n_leapfrog__),
    mean_acceptance_statistic = mean(chain_data$accept_stat__),
    divergences = sum(chain_data$divergent__)
  )
))

stopifnot(length(y) == 55L, nrow(diagnostics) == 4000L,
          sum(diagnostics$divergent__) == 0L,
          max(diagnostics$treedepth__) < 10L)
nuts_summary
```

```{r}
#| label: plot-provo-nuts-work
#| fig-cap: "Leapfrog work in four adapted NUTS chains for the passage-level Student-t model. No transition reached the maximum tree depth."
work <- aggregate(n_leapfrog__ ~ .chain + treedepth__, diagnostics, length)
names(work)[3] <- "transitions"

ggplot(work, aes(treedepth__, transitions, group = factor(.chain),
                 color = factor(.chain))) +
  geom_line(linewidth = .65) +
  geom_point(size = 1.5) +
  scale_color_grey(start = .15, end = .7) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = sort(unique(work$treedepth__))) +
  labs(x = "Tree depth", y = "Transitions", color = "Chain") +
  theme_classic(base_size = 12) +
  theme(legend.position = "top")
```

The maximum observed tree depth is `r max(diagnostics$treedepth__)`, and the
maximum leapfrog count is `r max(diagnostics$n_leapfrog__)`. These values
describe the four chains shown here; another posterior geometry could require
different path lengths.

**Identification** asks whether the observable-data distribution distinguishes
one parameter value from another. The [experimental-design chapter introduces
that connection between a target and observable
data](../experimental-design/index.qmd#what-you-should-already-know). A
parameter is **weakly identified** when substantially different values produce
very similar observable distributions. The posterior may then extend along a
broad or narrow ridge because the data change little as we move along that
combination of parameters. That shape can force NUTS to travel farther, but a
longer trajectory cannot create information absent from the likelihood.

NUTS chooses trajectory length within a transition. Warmup adaptation separately learns the step size and mass matrix. Increasing `max_treedepth` only permits more work; it does not repair inaccurate integration, poor geometry, or weak identification.

The target acceptance setting `.90` asks adaptation to favor smaller, more
accurate leapfrog steps than a lower target would. The depth cap of 10 limits
the size of the binary tree. Both settings regulate computation and leave the
model assumptions unchanged. Repeated saturation or divergences would
motivate diagnosis rather than automatic increases.

## Recap and forward link

1. Doubling tree depth grows one transition's candidate trajectory exponentially.
2. Endpoint and subtree checks stop growth when the path begins to reverse.
3. Multinomial selection retains one eligible state; internal tree states are not extra draws.
4. Depth and target-acceptance settings regulate computation but do not repair model geometry by themselves.

The [Stan page](stan.qmd#the-complete-program) gives the exact program and sampling call that generated these diagnostics.

## Check your understanding

1. What doubles when tree depth increases by one?
2. What sign indicates that an endpoint has turned back?
3. Why is only one state retained from a tree?
4. What does repeated maximum-depth saturation diagnose?

<details class="understanding-answers">
<summary>Answers</summary>

1. The intended number of leapfrog steps, and thus the path length, doubles. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
2. A negative endpoint dot product, $\Delta q^\mathsf T M^{-1}\rho^-<0$ or $\Delta q^\mathsf T M^{-1}\rho^+<0$, signals a turn back. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
3. The whole tree constructs one transition; retaining all internal states as draws would misrepresent their dependent selection mechanism. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
4. Repeated saturation indicates that the allowed trajectory length is truncating exploration, though it does not identify whether the cause is geometry, step size, or the depth cap. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->

</details>
